 USDA Gives SNAP Retailers an Extension on Stocking Rule
 New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he convinced the president to greenlight the extension to benefit small grocery-store owners. 
 By Rebekah Alvey 
 November 13, 2026

 --> November 13, 2026 – Small grocery-store owners will have more time to implement a federal rule updating stocking standards, easing concerns from farmers’ markets, corner stores, and bodegas about keeping their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) authorization.

 A U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) rule went into effect Nov. 4, updating the number and varieties of staple foods grocery stores accepting SNAP benefits must offer.
 Stores now have an additional 90 days to make necessary changes before the rule is enforced, following a conversation between New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and President Donald Trump.
 The rule doubles the number of required items, and makes other changes to which foods qualify as a staple. It aims to increase the amount of “healthy” foods in stores. But since the rule was finalized, anti-hunger groups and small-scale retailers have warned the rule could be too onerous and cause stores to lose SNAP authorization or even close down entirely .
 In recent months, groups and lawmakers have asked the USDA to delay the rule. This included a letter from Mamdani just weeks before the rule went into effect.
 “For corporate grocery giants these requirements posed little challenge, but the story was different for our neighborhood corner stores and bodegas,” Mamdani said during a press conference Friday afternoon. He said these shops are the “beating hearts” of many neighborhoods and a crucial access point for SNAP households.
 SNAP purchases are also crucial to bodegas’ survival, Mamdani said. In NYC, SNAP purchases can make up between 15 to 30 percent of a store’s total sales.
 But these challenges were not restricted to the city. Many grocery stores across the country have felt the impact of declining SNAP sales, and some have struggled to meet the new stocking standards.

 Sign up today Sign up today Shortly before the rule took effect, farmers’ markets learned some of them would also need to comply with the new standards and had asked the USDA for more time to come into compliance .
 The extension would last “at least” 90 days and help stores secure the necessary goods, storage equipment, and more to come into compliance, Mamdani said, adding that local agencies would work with the USDA to help store owners get the necessary outreach and resources for the rule.
 “We want to supply healthy food to our customers, and we also want to strive to be in compliance with every rule and regulation,” Amr Abozaid, director of small business services at the Yemeni American Merchants Association, said during the press conference. “But when the federal government puts a new complex rule and only gives us a few months to comply, they set us up for failure.” ( Link to this post .)
